blocks.x: Yeah, give your name.
Okay, let's go on. What's your name?
My name's Lester Santiago.
That's your full name?
Lester Lionel.
I see.
When were you born? What was your birth date?
I was born August 14, 1909.
That's a young man, huh?
Yeah.
Younger name? What part of town?
In New Orleans.
I mean, right in the...
In the Tramese. Wasteland and Roman.
Right around here.
Uh-huh.
Can you tell us about some of the very first music you ever heard? Did your parents play any instrument?

Well, when I was a kid, my Uncle Willie was with Bessie and Louis Armstrong. At that time, he used to visit my home and they would bring the instruments over on Sundays. Yep. And, uh, that made me take a liking to the music. My Uncle Willie was a banjo player. He played with P. Ron and Louis Caput and several of the old fellas. How old was he?
How much older than you? Do you know when he died? What was the date about?
Uh, Willie died in, uh, 1945.
And do you know about how old he was then?
Yeah, he was about, uh, about 50-age.
50-age. Was he born right here?
Yeah, he was born in New Orleans also. He's on, uh, North Robertson in Spain. Uh-huh.
I remember Bunk used to call him, once talked about him, called him to go over and see that Mexican. As if he were part Mexican. Was he part Mexican or Spanish?

Yeah, he was part Manila. His daddy was Manila, which my father was Manila, too. They had two brothers, Willie and my father. My father was named Albin. He also played a little guitar and mandolin at that time himself.
Your father did?
Yeah.
Did he play with any bands or just some stuff?

No, no. He just played for his own entertainment. My mother played piano and organ also. That's where we got the idea to about music. But I liked the drums on the beginning. And, uh, I'd taken the lessons with a neighbor of mine by the name of Bataulamy. And, uh, I was at the age of about 13. And, uh, so...
Did he play in any band that you remember?

He was playing with, uh, Renee and, uh, Sam Morgan and the bands at that time. And, uh, I was going to play the instrument pretty good. But the trouble is, the job that I played, I was so small, I couldn't carry the instrument around, so I decided to give it up. And I stuck to the piano. I have, uh, my oldest sister, she plays piano very well, right from my mother.
She's still living?
Yeah. She plays strictly by music. She can't play by ear at all.
Classical music or the popular music here?
Popular music. Um, as we grew up, my mother, she had, uh, 12 children. And as they went along with the piano, one tried to outdo the other. And they had, uh, a whole family of piano players.
There were 12 of you?
It was 12. And, uh, I had one brother that died, a boy now.
You've all heard of him.
Yeah, he's a wonderful piano player. And he was the first that worked at Hip Gunley when he started out, Famous Doe. He played there just piano and drum for a number of years.
So he's older or younger than you?
He's younger than me.
Younger. Did he have any lessons or pick it up himself?
No, he picked it up himself. He didn't have any lessons. I'd taken lessons with a girl by the name of May. And, uh, I was taking lessons with Willie Humphrey. And, uh, at that time...
You wrote a piano or some other instrument?
A piano. Uh, at that time, uh, a band leader by the name of Arnold Depes had a supreme band. And, uh, it was Talbot's, uh, brother-in-law. Alma Talbot.
Uh-huh.

I went to rehearsal with them and, uh, they seemed to like me. And I went to work with them, with their band. I played quite a number of years with them. Then, uh, Eddie Jackson, supreme, uh, band, was working on, uh, the music box, Crowlet and Canal.
Is that the tuba?

Ray tuba player. He used to play, uh, Tuxedo Brass Band. And, uh, I worked with him a while. Then I played lots of funerals and parades with them, playing the drums, too. So, after them, I went with Papa Celestan. As was, uh, I replaced with Jeanette when, after Jeanette got married and she was about to have her first child. And I just remained with the band until it broke up. And also played with Ridley Tuxedo and the Creole Serenators. I worked with them a long time. That's where I learned to play the vibes. Uh, Peter Bocais was playing trumpet and vibes. And he found it was a hard job to play both instruments. So, he taught me the vibes so I could relieve him. And...
Who else was in that band beside Peter?
They had, uh, Peter Bocais, Charlie Bocais, Henry Bocais. Louie Warnick was their manager. And, uh, this boy plays with, uh, with George Williams drums now.
Washington?
No, no. Little shot of...
Plays with, uh...
George Williams, uh, brass band.
He plays...
Sun White.
Sun White.
He was, uh, on drums at that time. We had a wonderful band. And they played all the country clubs and the hotels and everything.
Did you have a trombone in that band?
No, no trombone.
What did Warnick play?
Warnick was saxophone and clarinet. Yeah.
I never heard him on clarinet. I heard him on records with P-Rom and alto.

Well, he blowed nice clarinet, too. In other words, him and Willie used to double at one time on clarinet. He was a very good friend of William Humphrey. And, uh, from then, I scouted around with P-Rom. Played with P-Rom a while. After Louie Warnick died, the band broke up. Played with P-Rom. And up until he's dead. And, uh, ended up with Paul. I've been with Paul ever since.
How many years have you been with Paul? Paul, right?
Oh, I'm with Paul now. About eight years.
Mm-hmm.
I also played saxophone. I've taken a lesson with Emmanuel Cristo and Willie Humphrey Boyd.
What saxophone did you play?
Alto. Alto sax.
Did you play it professionally?
Yeah. I worked with it.
Spot jobs or regular?
No. Spot jobs. Funerals. A few dances and so forth.
Which brass bands have you played with?
I played with the Young Tuxedo. Played with Eureka. But, uh, the band I was organized to play with, uh, was George Williams. He's the one that started me back with the brass band.
So you usually played snare? Snare. Did you ever play? Do you play bass drumming?
No, I played snare all the time. I liked the snare. I've never seen the bass drum. I imagine I can play the bass drum. No, I know it's a beat.
I was going to ask you some more about your Uncle Willie. Which Kappa did he play with?
Freddie Kappa.
Freddie Kappa.
Uh-huh. Played with Louis Armstrong. P. Ron. Yeah. Buddy Bowden. Played with all the old fellas.
How old was he? When did he die, did you say?
About 68.
Yeah, about 68 years of age.
Did he ever talk to you? Tell you when he learned, who he learned from? Or?
No, he, uh, he really learned himself, uh, according to what my parents told me, he made his first banjo.
Okay, so we're talking about your Uncle Willie. He learned himself. You said mostly.
Yeah, mostly learned himself. Uh, kind of what my parents spoke to me, he said that he first made his own banjo. Oh.
Do you think he started on banjo or guitar when he started?

Uh, banjo he first started on. He changed to guitar. And I don't know what's his reason for quitting, but he was well recognized in the music field. Uh, the last record he made was, uh, with Kid Renee's band.
Yes, I have them. Uh-huh. Did he make any before that, you know?
Well, not that I know of. Uh-huh.
He may have made it. What did he make his banjo out of? Did they ever turn into?

Well, he, someone gave him the neck of a banjo, and, I don't know, he got around until he could get to the body part, and he put it together himself. And, it was a very good instrument because he played it in the bands for a number of years before he decided to buy one. He used to fix these mandolins and all that himself.
He played mandolin too?
Yeah, he was a wonderful mandolin player.
Did he ever play any piano, do you think?
No, no piano. Just, uh, string instruments.
How many people came over here from Manila? Many musicians?

Well, no, not that I know of. I know my grandparents are from the Manila Islands on my father's side. And my mother's, uh, on my mother's side, they're French people. My parents live down there, Seminar Parish, the Frenchman's down there.
Mm-hmm. Is your mother down there, Dad?
No, my mother's dead, and I asked my mother in 1940.

I don't like to bother you as much about your uncle, but since he's not here, that's really to talk to himself. If you can remember anything else he ever told you when you were a kid about the bands? He said he played with Buddy Bolden.
Buddy Bolden.
Did he ever tell you anything about Buddy Bolden or when he played with him?
No, not too much. More than a few men, I had a couple of pictures of bands that he played in at the time, and I would ask them questions concerning the fellas in the band.
Were any of those pictures around anymore? Do you think we could get copies, make new copies from them by photographing them?

I think I gave Paul one some time ago. Paul Barmerun. Mm-hmm. It was a pretty old picture when he used to wear these old-time uniforms. Like brass bands wear. They got fields and all these fellas on there.
Which fields is that? Yeah, the trombone player. The trombone player.
I don't know him at all.
He's been long gone, I'm sure.
Yeah.
We have one of your uncle playing with Paul and Albert Nicholas and Arnold Matoye at Tom Anderson's. That picture.
Tom Anderson's, yeah. He worked there a good while. He also played the board. Stephen Capitol. I played Stephen Capitol too with Pierron.
Was he with Pierron or Faye or who?

He, no, he was Pierron. At that time, Pierron had, had, uh, his, uh, Boccage, a whole Boccage band, which was Creole Serenade. It was with Pierron before Pierron died. And they organized Creole Serenade. It was set members of Pierron's orchestra.
Did you take Steve Lewis' place or was there somebody in there before you?
Uh, no. He had another fellow in there before me. I just remember his name now. He's dead also. You can lean back if you want to relax.
You don't have to lean back.
Yeah.
Did you ever know Dwight Newman?

Yeah, I knew Dwight. Uh, Dwight Newman, I replaced Dwight Newman with Eddie Jackson's orchestra on the music box. I also played, uh, uh, majority of the, uh, Dwight Newman's dance places, you know, the Jitney dances.
Mm-hmm.
One's up on Iberville, where were they?
Oh, yeah. It was on Iberville. There was one on St. Charles and Padres.
What was the name of these places? Uh, St. Charles and Padres, huh?
I just remember them. Mm-hmm.
Just another Jitney place. Yeah, Jitney.
Was there one down on the Charters and Royal different times? Did you ever play those?

Yeah, I worked over there, too. It had been so long, I can't just remember the name of them. Mm-hmm. I was quite a young kid at that time. I was in my early 20s. Mm-hmm. Yeah. Around 22, 21 years old. Wow.
Did you ever hear Freddie Keppard play when you were a boy?

Yeah, I was Freddie. I was quite a young kid. And around following funerals and advertisements on trucks. And at the time, they had furniture wagons. Used to follow the furniture wagons from corner to corner. And they used to buck one of their main corners for bucking. Mm-hmm. He drew the biggest crowd. My uncle used to play on the front of the wagon quite often. Well, I work with Manuel. I work with Manuel a good while. I work with Manuel out to the lake, Mellon Boy. I was still quite a young man then. I remember once we played a picnic out there. How about you? We had a very fine band. I think that was one of the first jobs I played with Paul. Manuel Perez had hired him. Had an old bass player named Joe Howard. You know Joe Howard?
I didn't know him. I knew about him. Yeah. Heard him on record.
He was playing bass with us at that time. One of the few old ones that I worked with.
I was going to ask you about an old bass player. Did you ever know Johnny Prudence?
Yeah, I knew no of him. I never did work with him. I just knew him as being a musician.

Did his wife? Did you ever know his wife? No, never met him. She lived somewhere near you, Glenny was telling me. Yeah. I'll have to look it up, you know. I thought maybe he knew. What was the first band you ever played with you, sir?
The first band? It was On All The Past.
That was the first, huh?

Yeah, On All The Past. Yeah, On All The Past. And I mixed it with Rene, Sam Morgan. I was having the majority of them afterwards, after I found out I could play, they used me. At that time, they was using Judge E. Parker. You know Judge E. Parker? Uh-huh. And a father by the name of Edward Johnson, he called him as a alias Plitsam. What? Plitsam. Plitsam. Red Caillou, he's also dead. Oh, it's old fellas.
What was Red Caillou's name? Did you know that?
No, I always called him Red Caillou. That's all I knew him about.
Probably wasn't his real name at all, I guess.
No, it's a alias name. Uh-huh. Well, he mostly played in the fast houses in the U. K. Ray and so forth. During the time, he really liked it.
What about your family? I wanted to get your brothers and sisters straight. Is Chani young?
Yeah, Chani's the baby. The baby girl. That's John Brunner's wife, the trumpet man.
And she's a pianist.
Yeah, she also plays.
Uh-huh. What year was Burnell born in about?
Burnell? Burnell was born in about 1915, around during the time of the storm. Burnell was born in about 1915.
And he wasn't even to play piano.
He was in his blood and he made a wonderful piano player. How young did he start? When he was a little kid? Oh yeah, much younger than me.
When he was around 12 years old, he was playing fine piano at that time.
He was around 12 years old. He was playing fine piano at that time.
You always had a piano at home to practice on?
Always had, yeah. My mother had an organ and a piano.
Did she ever help the children with the music sound?
Yeah, she would be doing her work in the kitchen, and if you made a bad note, she'd call you attention to it. She'd stop you and correct you.
Did you learn to read right away when you started in music?
No, no. I'll tell you what started me to take lessons. I made a trip with Harold Dajon on the SS Dixie. That's around 1929 or 30, I'd say. I traveled on the boat until about 32.
Where did that go?

From New Orleans to New York City. And while traveling on a ship, they decided that the band would have to play to entertain the passengers. And those people had their own music. So they presented me the music on one trip, and I told them I didn't know how to read. So they got someone from off the ship, a passenger, to play my part. So Harold told me, he said, well, Leslie said you're a fine piano player, but they're going to have to leave you go, he said, because you don't read. He said, I've been behind you to take up music. He said, it wouldn't cost you anything. And if you have enough friends around as musicians, they'll probably teach you for nothing. So that's when I started to take lessons. Well, after studying for about a month, I began to read. So I used to fight the parts with Harold Dajon. I still had the job. Fight the parts, and he found out that I was doing real good, and he helped me. And at that time, John Brunus, that was one of his first jobs that he had on the ship. He was a young boy right out of college. And Harold Dajon would teach both of us. Old numbers he would find out from the captain if anybody had anything to sing, and so forth. And we would call rehearsal on the ship. And he would play the melody on his saxophone. And I would try it on the piano. Some parts that I couldn't make, he'd teach it to me. And I went on and I started reading pretty good. So I kept the job until he laid us off. It was around 1932 when he laid us off. I found out then that you need to know something about music. You need to know how to read. I've been fighting it ever since. And I really improved. I made a headway by it. I played with plenty of reading bands. And with Peter on and all that you had to read. Because they had the music wrote. Played with Larry. In fact, now I play with any of them. It's called on me. You played with Larry?
Yeah, I worked with Larry too.
Who was Larry?
Who was Larry?
Who was Larry? He got the side of the syncopated. And what did he play?
What instrument?
He's a piano player.
What did he use too?
No, he mostly direct.
Oh, I see.
He stands in front of the band. Now and then he may play himself.
What about your brother Bernal? Did he read much or was he mostly... He didn't read at all.

He couldn't read at all. He tried it one time. And he was interfering with his fingering. He had such fast fingers he could play the Flight of the Bumblebee. All these hard numbers, sophisticated lady. Numbers like that he could play them. And that's where he features himself on these kind of pieces. See? He was working with him. So... When he tried to take up music he found out it was slowing up his fingering because the way the music was wrote was altogether different from the way he fingered the instrument and the way he liked. So he decided just to go off like that. And he met the best of them. He met Fat Wilder here at the fairground. And he met several other fellas, musicians. And they wanted to take him away but he never didn't want to leave home. He made one trip on the Dixie too when I was on there in New York. And he met Biddy Carl. He was supposed to have run several people off the piano. Paul and Danny Barker was in New York at that time. And Danny got a lot of malice in his head. He was bringing them around all these good players. And he would let Burnham play first. Then get one of those fellas to play behind him. And so I heard I wasn't there at the time. Paul told me the only fella that ran Burnham off the piano was Billy Carl. He's playing with Lewis right now. Well, when I made the trip with Paul to New York, at least we were storing all that section up that way. We went to Boston, Hartford, Connecticut, New York City. We played at Charles Paramount restaurant up there. And every Sunday evening we played against a different group. We met some strong players up that way. I also went to California with Paul. I think Paul played a lot of nice jobs the time that I've been with him. We've been on TV twice with Dave Galloway.
Oh, yeah.
We made a lot of recordings. We're on five different labels now.
That's a pretty lot. Did your brother ever make any records that you know of?
He made one. I think my second to the last sister has it at the house. I'll find out for him.
Seems to me some friend of mine, John Reed, was down here. I don't know if he recorded him on St. Louis Blues or something. I'd sure like to hear him, but I never got to hear him.
The record that she has, I think, is Deep in the Heart of Texas. A song, Deep in the Heart of Texas.
It was before they had tape recorders, but this friend, mind you, he worked for Victor and he had his own little home record. He might have been.
Yeah, it was one of these little machines that cut the records they self. Yeah, it was a blank record you put on and cut it.
When did he die? Let's see.
He died, it was around 1946, 1947. He died.
I've seen his grave. Yeah. I go on. It's over there in St. Louis.

Woody Groon, you know, Woody Groon, who made those records with your uncle, I think he maybe heard him too. I don't think he would hurt him at all. I'd sure like to hear him. What style did he play? Since we didn't get to hear him, can you describe him? Did he play all sorts of pieces or a lot of blues?

No, he played all sorts of music, classic and everything. All numbers like a sophisticated lady. All hard numbers like body and soul. And he was wonderful. He could play blues and jazz too. He's a wonderful piano player. He could imitate anyone.
He could play all sorts.

If you ask him to play something like Duke, he'd play Duke's records just like it was. Did he have a... But he still was more on the heart of Tatum and... A lot of fast fingers. Fat Wallace. Yeah, a lot of fast fingering.
How big was he? Did he have a big hand that he could play a lot of tents like Earl Hines played?
No, no. He had small hands. Small hands. Small hands with fast fingers. He could get over the piano.
What kind of bass would he use in his own style?
Well, he mostly would use the swinging bass at that time.
And how does that go?

Well... I mean... The way they play the piano now, they play one part of the piano, the center part of the piano, and they mix mostly all four chords. But at that time they had a swing bass, you swing from maybe the low B flat and form the B flat chord on the center part of the piano.
You mean you'd play one low note...
One low note... And then on chord? Yeah, it was three notes in the center of the piano. One low note and three in the center of the piano. That's the way it was.
Hit the lower and then octaves usually? That's right. Sometimes you make an after beat or...
Yeah. It mostly was hit on the beat.
Well, would you say his left hand was anything like Fat Swallow's left hand?
I'd say his hand was faster than Fat Swallow. He's right and left. Each one of them was just as fast as one of them.
But he would use that same style of left hand at these...

Well, he played different types of piano. In other words, he imitated very near anybody that he heard. He got a record of anyone. He listened at it. And after listening at the record once or twice, he set the piano and he'd be on there and play it like it.
I suppose he had a record of a full band. What could he do?

Yeah, at that time he would imitate... Lewis Armstrong was in full bloom with that mahogany hard stump and all that. Well, he played the mahogany hard stump just like Lewis played it on the record. Each man's part, he played it on the piano. If there was a bass solo in there, he played bass solo and saxophone solo and trumpet part. He played it just like the record was composed. That's the way he practiced playing. He'd take a record from Duke and play the record just like Duke made it.
Did he ever compose any pieces of his record?
Yeah, he had a few numbers, but I can't remember them now. My sister could give you more detail on that.
What is your sister's name?
Well, the one out there was Leonela Johnson. Her husband was a saxophone player too. His name was Edward Johnson.
So many Edward Johnsons. Yeah. You know?
Yeah, he was Edward Johnson number one. They used to call him number one and the other was...
Big Head was...
Big Head number two. He worked with George McCullin. Sax I did myself. Shots. I worked with all those folks. The WPA band. One time they had about 80-something other pieces in the band.
We'd like to go and talk to her and her husband both, you know, and everybody over there, you know, when it's convenient with them.
Well, I can make an appointment for you, ain't you?
Alright, that would be good, Bill. Yeah.
He's not playing no more, but he's got a good background. He traveled with ministry shows and...
I've heard so many people mention him.

Yeah, he gave it up for a true sickness. He's got a boy, there's two boys that's nice saxophone players now. One of them's going to Xavier, Lloyd and Edward. He's finished school and he plays a nice horn too.
I was saying something. You mentioned about May, taking lessons from May. Can you tell us anything about May? I've heard that name before.
Was your piano teacher?

Well, she played with some bands too. I don't know May's last name, but she's a better tall girl, you may know her. She worked with Ridley Tuxedo, that's where I knew her from. I used to replace her when she was working with Ridley. When she lay off like that, I replaced her. That's how I got to know Ridley. Do you remember Anna Barrett, when she worked with her? Yeah, I know. I know Anna Barrett. Is that before that or later? No, it's around the same time. I'd say before, even before. What did she? And Wilhelmina Barrett. I replaced it at the La Vida. I replaced it, not the La Vida, Alamo. Over McCoy's on Canal Street. I replaced the...
Yeah. What did she do?
You were talking about this pianist May that helped you. You say she played by music or what?
By music, strictly by music. She was a very good piano player and had long fingers. She played beautiful basses, all tense. Our style was on the order of Steve Lewis.
Well tell us some more about Steve Lewis in a minute too.

She, I think she was born over the lake, she was raised over the lake around where Rickard Lexus come from. And she came over here to work to different bands. It seemed as if she didn't take so well. But those that hired her was very well pleased with her because she could read all their music. There was plenty of bands that played songs by ear. She couldn't cut that unless they had the music to it. Couldn't get along so well. So I went back to Steve Lewis. When I first met Steve Lewis, I met him in the Hummin' Boy Cabaret. There was a cabaret on Ivorville and Moray.
A nice quiet place?
Well no, it was one of these hunky-tonks, as we call it.
Yeah. Which corner was that where Pete Lawless used to be on the lake uptown?

No, that was on the river uptown corner. They had strictly piano playing over there. That would go on day and night. That's where I first heard Steve and Manuel Moneta and Pete Marvin. They was on a party there one night. I was nothing but a kid that stole off and put on long pants to go around. And my brother taking me into the Hummin' Boy. And that's where Steve was playing. And later on my uncle Willie came in. He wasn't expecting to see me there, but since I was there, we made a jam section out of it. And he got me to play the piano and let Steve and them hear me. And from then on, Steve thought he could make something out of me. He used to pick me up every now and then. And we used to go out to the South Pole Club. And he would, uh, him and Piron would go out there and entertain people and make the extra money just violin and piano. So I would go out to the South Pole Club with the permission of my family and play in between.
Where was that? Is that near where Odois is?
That's way up around the riverfront now. At Colton Avenue, the end of Colton Avenue, up in that section there.
Up in Jefferson Parish?
Yes, beginning of Jefferson Parish, yeah.
Where's the protection levee they talk about? Yeah, that's right.

Is that where the levee's up in there? Exactly. And we had wonderful times up there. And, uh, that's how I become good friends with Piron. I used to go to places where they would be playing, like New Orleans Country Club and Metro Golf Club and so forth. I'd go out there and sit on a bandstand with them and things that I could play. They'd let me play with the band. Well, I got accustomed to the way the band played and had a fast year at that time. I caught on. And I ended up with Piron's band.
Somebody once told me that Steve Lewis was sort of the brains of the Piron band, as if he was the best musician there, helped arrange and maybe wrote a lot of those pieces.

Well, I'll tell you, Steve composed a lot of numbers of his own. He had special songs that he used to sing and the people went for his singing. He had a nice voice. On the order of Fats. What, Fat Pichon? Like, uh, Pichon would do his own, uh, his own numbers. Uh, Steve had his own numbers to do like that. And, uh, they would buck and they would give concerts. That's what made, uh, Steve Lewis so famous. Cause he had certain numbers that the band wouldn't play with him at all. He just would feature himself on the piano and the band would lay out and make a chord on the last. And people would listen to his singing.
Do you remember some of those special numbers that he played?
Uh, one of them was, uh, a song by the name of Woman, Aren't You Lie to Me. Uh, Mistreatin' Mama. Uh, he made several. Several numbers.
Did he have any special piano style? Anything different than other pianists here?
No, no, I wouldn't say. Each type was on, uh, the average piano player style.
Didn't have as much speed as your brother, I guess.

No, he didn't have as much, uh, fingering, but he was, uh, noted to have good basses. He had a walking bass, you recall. It's a double-wrapped bass he used to make in his playing that was wonderful. I makes it sometimes now myself. That's why I got it from him.
How old a man was he? When did he die? Do you remember?
Uh, Steve must have died around, uh, around 39 or 40. He was playing somewhere around Royal Street in the hood. When he died, he'd take a stroke.
Do you know how old he was about? Was he much older than, uh, uh, as old as Willie?
He was around in Willie Humphreys' class.
Willie Humphreys.
Yeah. He would be around 55, 56 years old. He was late 50s.
Did you ever make that double-wrapped bass on a record that you know of? No.
No, I never had. You know what I used to? I do it in my playing sometimes. I never thought of it while, while making records.
What pieces would you use? That in blues or just any piece?
Any piece. You use it in fast pieces or slow pieces.
Can you hum it a little over there? Show us what it's like here?

Yeah, you go, Like a beat on a snare drum, you know? Mm-hmm. In other words, it's a tent. Yeah, it's like you form a tent on a piano, but instead of hitting it in one lick, You break it down, you see? First, second, third.
Who would be the best pianist that you ever heard? Did you have a favorite? Did you have a favorite? Maybe your brother or anybody else? Or who would have been the greatest player you ever heard?
Well, I like Teddy Wilson, but I think Art Tatum was the best. I like Art Tatum a lot.
Of the fellows down here, who would be the best that you ever heard? Around here?
Mm-hmm. Well, I think my brother was. I'd throw in bouquets out there. Yeah, I understand. A lot of people would say that.
Yeah, I think he was the best piano player around the city.
Who was the best when you were a kid on piano and drums?
Did they use piano much when you were a kid in the band?
Yeah, they were Steve Lewis and Walter Pichon. They was about the best they had. And Faith Marvin, they were the most recognized piano players.
Well, who was the best for playing ear music? Ear music?
They had a father by the name of Lil Willie.
Lil Willie.

Yeah, he's from off of St. Lannan and North Durban. That's where he was living. But Willie was supposed to be one of the best piano players there was around the city. He made changes that you couldn't tell that he wasn't reading.
Did he play everything? Or just blues?
No, he played everything. He worked also with Rene and the bands.
I don't know his last name either. Is this a long-headed fellow?

Long-headed Willie. Used to call him Long-Head Willie, yeah. He was a nice piano player. At that time, the piano players was following them tents. We didn't play tents. They thought you couldn't play, you know. But it wasn't so. Some guys had short fingers, they couldn't finger tents. But they yet played. They had wonderful piano players at that time.
Any other good pianists that you can remember, even when you were a little kid, before you took up piano, when you were playing drums?

My uncle used to bring someone over home, followed by the name of Freeman. He was from Chicago. He was playing with Faith Marvin, I think my uncle was working with them. He was a wonderful piano player. I don't know what had become of him. Nah, he left away from me. I never see him anymore.
You were too young to get into the district and all, but do you remember Emmanuel Moneta, how you mentioned you heard him?

You see, all those people was my uncle's friends. And when they come from playing music, they might have been in different bands. Sometimes they played in the sound band, but they had their corners they would meet on. They had the wagon top on Sinan between Moray and Liberty. That was the headquarters for musicians. And they had the Herman Boy and they had the entertainers and they had Pete Lallis. Most of any of those four or five places, the folk could get around to and he'd find his friends there.
How did Fess play in those days? Fess?

Well, Fess was known for his reading. He's a good musician and he mostly would go around, his biggest money that he's made I imagine so was going around entertaining. He would be hired by people just to entertain by himself. He played wonderful piano for that. He worked with bands too.
Did he play a lot of rags or did he play? He played all the rags.
Climus Rag. Oh, he don't know.
Did he stick pretty much to the music or did he jazz him up a lot or what did he do?

Well, he could always read good. He was a first class musician, but he would get off the music and jazz too. He had these little things he would put in, little runs in between and so forth. I think he's a wonderful man.
There were some other older pianists before your time, I guess Tony Jackson. Did you ever hear him?
I always talk of him, but I don't know him personally.
He left here when you were six or seven years old anyway. Yeah. What about Alfred Wilson? I don't know him.
And Alfred Cahill, Carol.
It might be Carol or Cahill, I never could find out.
Who's that fella? Did you ever hear a guy named Buddy Carter or something like that?
Billy Carter?
No, Buddy Carter. Piano player.
Piano player.
Piano player?
No.
That may be his buddy, I don't know. I never could tell about that name. That name is familiar.
Jelly Roll talked about him. Did you ever hear Jelly Roll in person?
Yeah, I was small when I heard Jelly Roll. He was very, very small.
There's a white pianist used to be around here, Kid Ross. Did you ever hear him? Worked in the houses on Basin Street too, like Lula White's.

Well, one time I heard him in a speakeasy. It was on Domaine and Robinson. He came down to Buck Willie. Little Willie. Because all the piano players from all parts of town would look Willie up when they thought that he was strong enough, you see. And they tell me him and Willie tied up there for a while, now came in on the last of it. I heard about two, three numbers that he played. He was a nice piano player. Who won? Well, everybody was playing for Willie. Willie had the reputation at that time. I think that Willie was the best. Long-haired Willie.
Was he who was it? Buzzy Williams, another white pianist?
He was Kid Ross's roommate. Yeah. I don't know if you know him. I don't know him.
What was the district like? Was there anything left there when you were, say, 15 years old and started going around there? Were there any of the houses left on Basin Street?
Yeah, they still had the houses. All little cribs, little one-rowed cribs. Still going in the 20s.
Yeah.

They still had the cabaretts, but they began to tighten down on them a little. The entertainers was the last one that closed. With the music and entertainers. They were the last one. They were the last one. They were the last one.
They were the last one. They were the last one. They were the last one.
What was it like? Did they have a band there? This piano? Well, they kept with a band there. Oh, NAM bands. The leading bands of the city. Rene and Buddy Petit and Sam Morgan.
What did the entertainers close about?
Oh, I see. Entertainers opened in 27. 1927 it still was open, but it wasn't, it was kind of being run decent then, you see. That's terrible.
Yeah.
But when I first know the entertainers, they had all kinds of shows going on and that. It was more of a bull ass than anything else. A few from all over. Yeah. Came there, white and colored.
But there wasn't any other club like it. That was the only one left? Was it?
Well, Pete Lawless, Pete Lawless closed before the entertainers. The entertainers was the last one.
Do you remember Nancy Hanks' saloon? It was up on that corner too, where Pete Lawless, somebody told me once, I'm not sure. Nancy Hanks.
Nancy Hanks.
It was a saloon, but they had music.
They were in Iberville and Basin.
Or Moray in Iberville, someplace up in there. Might have been at Liberty. Maybe at Liberty Street.
There was one there at Liberty Street, but it wasn't popular. I guess that's why I don't know too much about it.
You don't remember the old place like Rice's, I guess, and Appadise?
Yeah, I would talk of it, but I never went around them. What happened before you were in time? Before my time. Before my time.
Say, you said the entertainers, white and colored both came in. They'd mix it up.
Yeah, they'd mix it up.
Musicians would get together and jam and sit at the table together.

Jam and people would come up in there, just like doing on Boyfriend Street. They'd come to hear the music. They had a little platform for those who wanted to dance. They had a certain time of night they would put over the show. But that would run all night. It might run until 10 or 11 o'clock the next day, as long as there was people in there that band worked. And you wouldn't get any more for it. It just was in their contract, as long as there was people in the place, they would go ahead and work. No knocking off time. And Saturday wasn't too much at that time, but three hours a night.
Did they get pretty good tips or not?
Yeah, maybe the tips. They mostly live on their tips.
Well, I think, what about the Big 25 in your time? Was there music there or just the hangout for musicians and what happened?
No, they had music. They mostly had three, four pieces there. It was three good man's that they had. They had 피shaw and Alfred Williams and Charlie Bocage on banjo. It was three good pieces they had.
Where was the band? Was it in the main room or was it in the back room?
in the back. They had the bar to the front and the nightclub in the back.
Was that near the coach table where the band was?

Around where they used to have the coach and the dice. In other words, they was petitioned off. They had a certain section of the building for gambling, and the nightclub, and the bar. That's the way it worked in there.

Do you remember a little room they called the wine room? That was about 40 years ago. Way back, the bunk in Tony Jackson, they called the wine room where they had a piano just for musicians. Nobody allowed in that room. Do you still have that in your time?

Well, in this particular... In 25? In 25, yeah, yeah. There was a little separate booth. They had a piano in there, and the piano player would take just his bunch and go in there and lock the doors. Nobody else was supposed to come in there. Unless they was invited.
How big was that? As big as this room or half?
Well, I'd say a room around 9 by 12.
That's a little fun.

Yeah, they had a table in there and a piano, and they'd sit down at the table and play the piano and listen. But they could hear the piano. It just was a wall petitioned off, you know, and the top was open and the music was still...
All over.
The girls dancing there? No, they were just a little table, sit down there and drink, you see. They could dance on the table, ain't they? Maybe so.
You know, they used to... All kinds of things. All the piano sounders.
Oh, well, they had these old upright pianos at that time, old pianolists and... It wasn't fine-sounding pianos like they got now, they're grand.
They still had that little room when they had the band there, like when Peter Boccage and all of them were there, they still had the other little piano in there?

Yeah, yeah. Even when they had the nightclub, that little room was for private guests. If there was any private bunch that you had, wanted to hear you or something like that, you'd get the permission from the bartender, he'd give you the key and you'd go in there and entertain whoever you wanted on the piano. That's how these fellas got interviewed and all that at that time, and come and listen at them. I'm more than sure, that's how Pierron got to go to New York one time. He's from over there.
There were many white people that went in there or not?
Yeah, yeah, many white people.
I think William Faulkner used to go in there.

Well, they had their fathers, you see. Those people used to follow Steve all over. And anywhere Steve would be when they got ready for a party, so there was a bunch out having a good time, they'd search up for Steve. And they knew Steve's headquarters. The entertainers, the humming boys, the B-25s, were by the Waggon Top for the Astoria. They would go over these places and search for Steve.
What was the Waggon Top?

The Waggon Top was on St. Peter, between Marie and Liberty. There was a shed where they used to keep horses years ago. And stables, you know? They'd fix it up and open up a ballroom in there. They had a bandstand in there. These fellas would knock off and wait. They'd have their jam session in there. They'd all get their instruments out and just play to Dick. Every 10 or 11 o'clock in the day, they'd still be blowing at one another. And that's Dick. I had some other questions.
I wondered if you could tell us a little bit about drummers. Since you were a drummer, who were the best drummers? Who did you like? And who helped you and all that on drums?
Well, I liked it in them times with Ernest Rapinoe.
What did he play on the street? Bass drum or snare?

He played bass and snare, both. He was a member of the Tuxedo band at that time. That's the time of the old Tuxedo with Paul's daddy and all that in there. Tass' daddy. He had a wonderful band and he was a wonderful bass drum player and also a snare, a good reading drummer. He's from out of Peter Lawrence Orchestra too. And Louis Contrail's daddy, old man Contrail. Well, that was one of the two of the best leading drummers they had around here at that
time. Who had the best role?
I'd say Contrail. Old man Contrail had the best role. That's what they said. He wrote it on a snare, it sounded like it was tin paper. Wonderful drummer. That was awesome.
What kind of drums did he use? Pretty deep one or big? Do you remember anything about it?

No, he drummed, I have a snare drum now that I use for playing the fumes and parades. It's called a duplex. Oh yes. One of the old time duplex. The drum that he had has those strings on it and the ropes.
I believe Alfred Williams still has one. He has.
Well, I got one now. I'm one of the only fellas. I know Happy had one like I have. I just out of me and Happy had.
Wooden shell or metal?
Mine is wooden shell. Wooden shell. Wooden shell but I got iron clamps on it, you know. Sure. But it was a wonderful drum.
I forgot what you told us when you started on drums. Did you take lessons much or how did you get started on drums?

No, I just used to practice on this fella. My father's drum, he was neighbors of mine and he used to have his drums rigged up at all times. And my oldest brother Harold, he would go over and play the piano and probably play his drums and I'd get on him and he'd start showing me. And I got so I could play the drums really good. But I never take lessons on drums.
Who was the fella next door?
His name was Batalami.
Well that's right, you mentioned him.
Batalami, yeah.
But I mean his full name was he?
Is he related to Dave, Batalami? No, his name was Lionel I think if I'm not mistaken. Lionel Batalami. He died quite a young man. Didn't play but a few years but he was a really good drummer.
You ever hear of Red Happy on drums? Oh yeah, yeah.
Yeah, a good friend of mine is Red Happy. Happy was a nice drummer too. He was considered one of the best himself. He was an ace on the street.
What did he play on the street?
He played bass drum too on the street. How did he play?
What about Black Benny? Some people talk like he's a great drummer.

Black Benny. People think that Black Benny was the best bass drum player they had on the street. But me, I liked it in the Orange Trepan. He's a better time keeper. And Benny had that way of clowning on the streets and making a lot of motions. That wasn't the people. He'd be playing too. They had nice drums. If I had to pick between the two I think it would be Trepanion. He's the best drummer. When he set that time, the time stood there.
Did you ever hear Mac Murray on the streets?
No.
I never heard. What about Mac Lacey? Little Mac they called him.
Little Jim. I wonder if it's the same part that I have in mind. You used to call him Little Jim. Is he here?
No, that's another guy. I know Little Jim.

I would work with Little Jim just before he passed. We played out at Seuss Barren, a parade out there. I played with John Casimir's band that had him. And again, I worked with him a couple of carnivals ago. He was coming up with a girlfriend. He'll know him. He'll know him. He'll know him. He was a pretty good little drummer too. I don't know this part you talking about.
I wanted to ask you, when did you first make a record? Either homemade or?

No. I made a few homemade records like my brother Boy now. But the first record I really made that worked while I was one with Celestan. I made the Josephine with Celestan. He made two Josephines. I think I made one and Jeanette made one. First of Sam and Ryan.
Well did you make the one, the recent one or the one in the 20s?
I made the old one. You made the old one in the 20s?
I made the old one. Do you remember what label they put it on?
I don't know.
I don't know if it was OK or I think it was OK label. Could it have been in Columbia?
Do you know? There was one on Columbia, I believe you.

I just remember what label it was on. Well we can check who was in the band then. Well they had Bill Matthews in the band. They had Guy Kelly. They had Rick Carter and Alexis. They had myself. They had uh…
Three trumpets huh?
Yeah. They had Lee Collins too in the band. Yeah.
Was Lee on the record too you think or just playing?
Yeah. The whole band, the big band. He had somewhere around 18 pieces in that band. They had uh… Marara. Marara on the bass. They had sales. You know sales?
Where is it? Guitar or band?
They played with Snooker Russell. He was in the band too. That's Manuel Sales. Manuel Sales. I mentioned Rick Carter. Yeah. They had a lot of us.
Who was the alto player? Uh…

Hall that's playing tenor saxophone now. Clarence? Clarence Hall. He used to be in his band. Yeah. Him and his brother. They had two brothers. I see Robert and Clarence. Yeah. Clarence Hall. Yeah. Uh…
Now, do you remember any other tunes you made with Celestan other than my Joseph? No.
Only that one record. I just remember it was on the other side. Uh huh.
Is there a singer? Who sang?
Celestan sang himself on that. Oh yeah.
Did you know Ferdinand Joseph? He used to sing some with Celestan.
Uh, Ferdinand Joseph, yeah, he was a singer. That's the world that Joseph brought him.
Is that right?
Yeah.
He brought him. I never thought that.
Wills Joseph's drummer. Which Joseph?
Wills Joseph.
I don't know him.
Uh, we had Eddie Pearson on the trombone, uh, at that time and a fellow by the name of Yank. Who was this with? The trombone. We, uh, with Celestan. And, uh… When did Yank die? Do you know?
Our buddy Johnson, either one of those trombones, his brothers? Uh, Yank died. I'd say it must have been around 1938.
Uh, yeah, because I worked with him around that time. He was in real good trombone player too.
Uh, back to Rene, I forgot to ask you who was in the band when he played with Rene.

When I played with Rene? Uh-huh. Well, he had a, uh, Bad Joe play by the name of Son. You see who else he had. He had his brother Joe on drums. He had, uh, McLean on bass. On, uh, guitar at that time. Uh-huh. Who else? The trombone? The trombone, they… What do you call this for? They died, uh…
They go over the river.
Hmm. Died recently.
Comboin. John Bowman.
Johnny Lindsay's the only one I can pick up. No. The trombone. Across the river… Mm-hm.
Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Died recently.
Died recently… Died recently…
Died recently…
Died recently… Died recently… Died recently…
Died recently… Died recently…
Died recently… Died recently… Died recently… Was that saxophone or clarinet? No clarinet. We had Big Eye Lowry on clarinet.
That was Nelson. Eddie Vincent was from across the ground, but that was...
He died years ago in Chicago. Yeah, I know this one.
Joe Avery. Joe Avery. Oh man, Joe Avery.
He's from Wagamond. Yeah.
